doc.title: Byron Stripling interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 25, 1998 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Gospel feeling and his grandmother getting the spirit
summary: Church music had little improvisation, but he saw the power of it in his grandmother shouting at a few bars of a hymn, which taught him what music can do.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: When the music was used in the church, was it fairly strict to follow the music or was there a bit of improvising that went on in a Gospel sense?

In the Gospel part yeah there was definitely some, but more than the varying of improvisation because a lot of — I’ve got to be honest — my impression is that a lot of music claims to have improvisation, I mean you’ll get classical people that say, you might have heard people on T.V. say on panels with jazz musicians, “Oh yeah, I improvise too as a classical musician; I put my trills in different places and I do this.” And Gospel improvises, rock musicians improvise, but jazz is a whole other level of improvisation. So in the jazz sense we weren’t improvising but the thing I think with Gospel music was the feeling was certainly there. And for me, again you realize the power of the music, when I would see people like my grandmother, who never had a high school education even, who was a poor speller and a poor reader, but yet she put three of her children through college through just working her ass off. And when she would go to church and all they would do was play about four bars of one of her favorite hymns, and she would begin to shout. Now that is confusing to a young person, it’s like walking in when you’re young and seeing somebody making love. You don’t really know what that is. And it’s the same with seeing your mother or your grandmother get the spirit in the Baptist church. What is that? And it was only later I was like starting to realize, she’s like © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

giving everything up to the Lord. She’s been working her behind off. She’s very happy, her children are not in jail, that she was able to provide a better way for them, for her kids. And this is such joy for her and she thanks God for it. But it took me a long time. Because all I knew was, “Mom, Grandma’s freaking me out, she’s over there screaming and shouting and I don’t know why.” Think about that, it’s a weird feeling for a kid, it’s all those impressions you get when you’re a kid that stick in your mind, those kind of impressions, and the fact that the music was that powerful and could do that to her was very interesting to me. And so when you have experiences like that with music, and I know in my own life and I’m sure in your life, you’ve had music sort of bring you out of depressions, music gives you a high, and it’s really a powerful anchor that can give you the spirit of what you need to do. And I think that’s why you and I and every other great musician are in this business. It’s not for money it’s for the feeling that it gives us.
